sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

Greyhollow hangs on the mountainside like a lantern on a nail — a mining town of slate roofs and smoke, where the Anvil Father is honored in every forge-song and the dead are buried with hammer-signs on their eyes. For six years Brakka Ironvein stood guard at its temple, and if the work was quiet, it was honest. Quiet is over now.

Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, sealed since Brakka's grandsire's time. None came back. Last night a fourth man climbed out of that dark alone, raving about "lights that walk," and died before dawn with the words still on his lips. The town council has no patience left for ghosts: at sunrise tomorrow, they brick the entrance shut, living miners or not.

So the prior, old Hessa, came to Brakka with a lantern and a plain request. Bring back whoever can still be brought back. Before the mortar dries.

Now it is late afternoon, the light going copper and low. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a black square cut into grey rock, the borrowed hooded lantern in one hand and its flame guttering in the cold wind that comes up out of the hill — a wind that smells faintly of wet iron. Around the entrance, the council's masons have already stacked brick and mortar for the morning. Inside: timber shoring, old rail lines half-buried in rubble, and darkness your eyes can't shape.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka checks the lantern's oil and the hood, then crouches at the mine mouth to look over the rail lines and the floor just inside for fresh boot prints or drag marks from the three miners. "Anvil Father, light my way," he mutters, and then he draws his shield up and steps in slowly, keeping the lantern low and listening for anything besides the wind.

transcript.text: time: 10 minutes later: Day 1, 5:20 PM; timer Hooded lantern (borrowed, lit): 6 hours

The wind swallows your prayer, but the Anvil Father has heard worse from you, and you know the old dwarf's habit of noticing.

The lantern's oil is better than half full — Hessa filled it herself — and the hood throws a clean circle of light when you open it. The mine mouth was sealed with a dry-stone wall, and it's been pulled down from the inside edge, loose stones scattered outward onto the track. You crouch over the rails.

You're no tracker, but a mine floor is honest ground. You make out boot prints in the dust between the sleepers: two sets walking in, side by side, then a third a step behind, heavier. Five, six strides, and the dark takes them. What you don't see is harder to miss — no prints coming back. Just one set, deep and staggering, heels dug in, going out. Someone walked out of here last night by main strength. Beyond the drip line your light falls on a scatter of broken shale and old timber shoring, and beyond that the tunnel bends left and down.

You step in. Ten paces and the daylight behind you is a coin of copper; twenty and it's a Memory. The wind dies at the bend, and in the quiet there's water somewhere below, a slow tapping, and — when you stop to let your ears work — something else. Far down and faint, a rhythmic scrape, like a shovel or a boot-drag on stone. It stops. It does not start again while you listen.

The tunnel slopes gently down, rails half-swallowed by rubble, the roof good dwarven work — old but sound. Twenty yards in, wedged in a crack in the wall, you find the first sign of the miners: a hand-lamp, its oil burned out, abandoned upright like a man meant to come back for it.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka pockets the dead hand-lamp, since it may be worth showing Hessa or the miners' families, and checks it for a name mark or a tally scratched into the base. Then he goes on down the slope with shield ready and the lantern hooded to a narrow beam, stopping at the bend to listen for that scrape again. "Hello the tunnel! Brakka Ironvein of the Anvil Father's temple. Hessa sent me to bring you home!" he calls, low but clear.

The hand-lamp is dwarven make, temple-familiar — the sort the old workings' original crews carried — but the base is crusted with a century of grime, and whatever's scratched there won't give itself up in this half-dark. You pocket it anyway. A wire brush at the temple forge would find it, and a name on the base is a name to a family.

You narrow the hood to a blade of light and go on. The bend takes you out of the wind's reach entirely, and the mountain closes in around you like a held breath: cold, still, only that far-off water ticking somewhere below.

At the bend you stop and listen. The scrape doesn't come again. Whatever made it either stopped, or is being still because it heard you.

You call. Your voice goes down the tunnel ahead of your light, and the echo comes back thinner and thinner — "home... home..." — until it dies. Then, from a long way below, an answer. There is one, you're sure of it: a voice, faint as a thought. But there are no words in it. Just a sound, held low, rising at the end almost like a question. It comes again, closer in your memory than your ears would have it.

And down the slope, far past the reach of your lantern, a light appears. One small light the color of starlight through ice, hanging at about the height of a lamp in a man's hand. It doesn't flicker like flame. It sways — once, gently, side to side — the way a swinging lamp would. Then it stands perfectly still, as if it had noticed you noticing.

The slope continues down. Between you and the light, the timber shoring gets older and more broken, and there are side galleries, black mouths cut in the walls, some gated with rotten boards.

Brakka keeps the lantern hooded and holds still a moment, then answers low and even: "I'm Brakka, from the temple. If you're one of the miners, show yourself slow, and no one gets hurt." Your words go down the tunnel and get no answer but that held-breath quiet. But the light hears you, sure as iron: the moment your boot finds the next sleeper, it drifts back a few yards — always a few yards, always out of your lantern's reach, never so far that you lose it.

You keep to the wall. With your ears sharp and your pace slow, the galleries give you what they have. Most are dead: black mouths and rotten gate-boards, nothing inside but older dark. Near one, an inch of water lies flat as a coin. In another, your lantern picks out a wheelbarrow rusted to lace. But the third gallery on the right is different, and your eyes stop on it: the dust on its threshold is cut through. Footprints — several sets, days old but honest-booted, going in. Not coming out. Just inside the gate, half-hidden by a fallen board, someone has dropped a pick. Laid down, not thrown — the head resting neat on a stone heap.

And one more thing, the kind you only get for standing still and trusting your ears: when you pass the cut galleries, the far water-sound changes. Not louder. Closer, each time, the way it would if the workings below were flooding down toward the level you're walking.

The pale light waits while you examine all this. It has waited at the mouth of that third gallery too, so that you'd find it — you'd swear to that, before the Anvil Father's own anvil. Then it moves on, and this time it swings left, away from the main slope, down a narrower drift where the rails end in a wall of collapsed stone with a gap torn through it, a man-sized gap, edges sharp and pale as bone. The light hangs on the far side of the gap.

It's colder here. Your breath smokes. And from beyond the collapse, very faint, comes the sound of knocking — slow, spaced, deliberate. Three knocks. A pause the length of a held breath. Three knocks.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka steps into the third gallery first, since the miners' prints lead there, and quietly asks, "Anyone in here? Knock if you can't speak." He studies the prints and the laid-down pick, then listens hard, comparing that three-and-pause knocking with whatever's in the gallery.

The gallery answers you with a word.

You step through the gate, and your call goes down twenty yards of honest dwarework and comes back with nothing living in it. No answering knock from in here. But your ears, sharpened by twenty minutes of that mountain's silence, catch where the knocking actually lives: not down this gallery's length but through the rock, as if the knocker were somewhere beyond the collapse the pale light guards, under the broken stone that lies between you and it. The same rhythm. Three, a held breath, three. Patient. Continued.

The prints tell their story plainly now. Three men walked in, spread out, working — boot heels worn in a steady tramp along the left rail. Then, a quarter of the way in, something changes. A scuff-turn, feet planted wide. Two sets of prints stand close together for a stride. And the third man's prints never go past that — his last few strides shorten, like a man slowing down while he watched something. From there, there are no more prints of his at all. Just a brushed line through the dust, wide as two boots dragged sidelong, faintly toward the gallery's far dark.

The pick was laid down by a careful man. And by the wall where he stopped, at exactly the height of a dwarf's resting knuckles, the rock is smeared with soot — and the soot carries words, drawn in a thick, shaking hand:

DO NOT FOLLOW THE LIGHTS

The same hand, smaller, under it: THE SEAM IS A LIE

Out at the drift, the pale light still hangs by the gap in the collapse. It hasn't followed you in here. And the knocking goes on beneath your feet: three, a breath, three — the way a tired man signals that he is still alive.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka reads the soot message twice and mutters, "Someone down there wanted me warned, and someone's still knocking, so he's alive." He follows the dragged line toward the gallery's far dark, lantern low and shield up, checking the floor and walls for the missing man and for any sign of what "the seam" might mean.

The drag line runs the gallery's length, steady, unhurried, past empty ore-carts and a roofed stretch where the shoring is undercut with old tool marks. Your lantern pools on the floor ahead. And at the gallery's dead end you find him.

He sits against the rock with his back straight, hands in his lap, like a man resting after shift. A human, young, beard gone white with frost, hair frosted too, in a miner's leathers. He is alive — you see the slow fog of his breath — but there is frost on his lips that his breath does not melt. His eyes are open, fixed on the wall beside him, and they do not move when your light falls on them.

You follow his gaze to the wall, and your stomach drops to your boots. The rock is veined. A seam of grey-white stone runs branching through it like winter lightning, and the whole of it glows from within — the same color as the pale light. It doesn't shimmer like mineral caught in a flame. It glows, gently, as if lit from a room behind the stone. Beautiful, if you let it be. Your dwarf's bones know stone, and these workings should hold nothing like it.

The miner doesn't seem to hear his name when you mean to speak it. His lips move. You lean close. He is whispering, over and over, barely a sound: "It's pretty. Don't look away. It's pretty. Don't look away." He is cold as the wall. Frost has built on the folds of his clothes, thick, as if his breath had been freezing on him for hours. And away at the gallery's far end, from beneath your feet, the knocking under the rock still goes on: three, a breath, three.

He's alive, but he cannot walk, and the rock he worships is beside him.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka steps between the miner and the glowing seam, shield up to block the line of sight, and keeps his own eyes on the man's face rather than the stone. "Look at me, friend. Look at me, not the wall," he says, then tries to gently turn the man's head away and cover his eyes with a cloak or hand before hauling him up over his shoulder to carry him out.

Your shield goes up between the man and the glowing vein, and you thank the Anvil Father for dwarves who made shields wide.

At first nothing happens. The man keeps whispering to the stone over the shield's rim — "don't look away, it's pretty, don't look away" — and his eyes strain sideways like a drunk resisting sleep. Then you put your fingers on his jaw, gently, and turn his face to you, and you keep your own eyes on his — grey, cracked at the rims, and empty as stopped windows — and you talk to him the way you'd talk to a frightened apprentice at the forge.

He blinks. The whisper stops. And then the mountain gives him back.

The shivering is worse than any trance — sudden, whole-body, teeth-cracking. His eyes fill, and for a heartbeat they're just a cold young man's eyes, and they see you. "You're... you're real." A wrecked voice, from a frosted throat. "Toma," he gets out, gripping your vambrace with feeble strength. "Toma's under the fall. He was knocking. Two days — two days he knocked." His face crumples. "Merrick followed the seam downhill and the pretty lights came out of the wall and — don't take me past the lights. They don't touch you if you don't look. They let you walk if you don't look."

He can barely stand, and he is close to weeping, and he weighs nothing a cold man shouldn't. Getting him over your shoulder with chain mail and shield will be slow work — half pace, at best, and both hands spoken for.

The knocking under the rock goes on: three, a breath, three. Behind you both, at the gallery's mouth, out along the drift — maybe forty yards — the pale light still hangs beside the torn gap in the collapse. Waiting. As if it had all the time in the world, because down here it does.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka drapes his cloak over the man's head and shoulders, then asks quietly, "What's your name, friend? And can you tell me how to reach Toma, or where Merrick went?" He listens for the answer before hauling him up, planning to carry him out to the mine mouth, then come back for Toma with rope and help from the temple before the mortar dries.

You give the lights the courtesy they were fishing for: none at all. Eyes on the ties, shield edge up like a blinder, Odo's weight shifting with every step, you walk the rails up-slope.

It's the longest walk of your six years in this town. The near light drifts alongside you — you see it only as a pale stain at the rim of your vision, just past the shield's edge — and it stays with you a dozen yards, patient, swaying gently. Once it comes so close the light of it warms the back of your hand, and once you hear something — not a voice, a sound like slow breathing through a crack, getting a half-step ahead, as if it were looking for somewhere to be seen from. You keep your eyes on the iron. So do the rails. And the slope goes up.

It tries one trick: it swings out ahead of you and hangs low over the track, right where you must look to see your footing. But it doesn't bank on dwarves. Dwarves count ties, and pattern is pattern — you walk blind-true by the rail's hum under your boot and the memory of every sleeper you crossed coming down. The moment passes. The lights let you go.

Maybe they simply let you, and that is the worst thought of the walk. But nothing touches you, and nothing touches Odo, and his shivering under your hands is a live man's shivering.

Ten minutes past the bend, you feel the wind before you believe it, and then the mine mouth's black square has stars in it, and you are out. Night has come down while you were below, and the cold outside is a friend after the cold in the rock. Bricks wait in their stacks. The masons have gone home to supper, lantern-bearers' windows shine in Greyhollow above, and the temple is a ten-minute climb through town lanes, its forge-window lit — Hessa keeps late hours.

You set Odo down against a stack of council brick, wrapped in your cloak, and he clutches your arm with both hands now, strength coming back as fear goes. "Hessa," he says through chattering teeth. "Get her. Tell her — three lights, and they've got the deep workings, and Toma's under the fall, and the seam is the worst of it. Tell her Merrick took samples. He had them in his satchel, brass sample-boxes."

Sunrise is a little under eleven hours away.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka wraps Odo's cloak tighter and says, "Stay put, Odo, and keep warm. I'm bringing Hessa and help, and Toma isn't getting bricked in while he's still knocking." He jogs up the lane to the temple, planning to rouse Hessa, ask for healers, rope, picks, and any volunteers, and to hold the masons off until Toma's out.

"The Anvil Father keep you, Odo — I'll be back before the mortar's mixed." He nods up at you, wrapped like a bundle of washing against the brick stack, and you go up the lanes at a smith's jog, boots ringing on frozen cobbles, lamplit windows sliding past overhead.

The temple's side door latch lifts to your hand — six years of right. The forge-room is warm, the banked fire breathing, and it's Hessa you find first, as you knew you would: awake, at her desk over parish rolls, spectacles pushed up into white braids. She listens the way the old do, without interruption, while you give it all — the prints, the soot warning, the seam, Odo's trance, three lights, Toma's knocking, Merrick gone down the deep stair with brass sample-boxes.

The sample-boxes stop her like a nail driven flush. "Rocks that shine in the dark," she says slowly, taking her spectacles down. "There's a hymn the old folk stopped singing before your grandsire was whelped, about lights in the north galleries, and men following them and coming back wrong. I thought it was a way of teaching children to keep out of bad air." She looks at you for a long moment. "Fetch Master Stoner's ledger-chest from the vestry, then. No — first things first."

First things, by Hessa's ordering: two lay brothers go down the hill with cloaks, a hand-cart and a brazier-pot of broth for Odo at once. From the guard-store she gives you what you asked for: a second good rope, two picks, a sledge, wedges, and three crowbars. And she does not stop there — she lays a hand on the shoulder of a broad, quiet dwarf who had come in on the bell-hour to bank the forge: Veylin, a temple hand of your own watch, whom you've shared lamplight with on night rounds for years, and the strongest back in the parish. He hears the whole thing, rubs his beard once, and says only: "I was born to this kind of foolishness, then," and starts pulling his coat on.

"And the council," Hessa says, harder now. "Sunrise is sunrise and their word is their word, but you'll have me behind you tonight, and every hammer in the temple. Go. The clock's yours. Master Stoner's ledger and the old hymn will be waiting when you're back for them."

Downstairs, Hessa's letter sits before the council's head — the town will know by midnight that the temple claims the mine mouth, and lives may lie buried in it.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka shoulders the rope and tools, nods to Veylin, and says, "Stay close and eyes on the floor when the lights show, friend. Don't look at them, no matter what they do." Before leaving he asks Hessa, "Anything in that old hymn about what turns them back, light or fire or a blessing of the Anvil Father? And could you send one of the lay brothers to wire-brush the base of the hand-lamp I found, there may be a miner's name on it."

Hessa thinks while you load the tools, then shakes her head. "Turning back. If the hymn said, Brakka, would a mine have been sealed with the words still in everyone's mouth?" She recites a fragment anyway, from somewhere deep: "'Keep to the wholesome dark, ye dwarrows all; the glitter that breathes is not thy father's spark; look to the anvil, not the bed of ore.'" She shrugs, small and old. "Advice, not remedy. But Master Stoner closed the north workings himself, and wrote why, somewhere in that chest. If a thing drives glitter back, he would have noted it, because he'd have had to live beside it. Get it when you come up — or send Veylin for it if you're loath to leave."

"And the lamp — done." A lay brother already has it out of your pack, wire brush in hand; by the time you've shouldered the ropes she calls him over and squints at the cleaned base. Her face goes strange. She says one word — "Corbray" — and sets the lamp down softly, as if it were heavy. "That's the name scratched there. Corbray. Older than Toma's whole family. That lamp went down with the first crews a generation back. Which means somebody was down there before the miners, Brakka — or something kept a lamp for sixty years."

She doesn't follow that thought any further, and neither should you, tonight. "Go. The Father walks with the thorough."

Veylin falls in beside you — chain mail, shield, warhammer, a sledge over one shoulder, calm as a feed trough — and repeats your rule back to you word for word, which is how you know it took: "Eyes to the floor. If I feel pretty, I look at you."

Broth and brazier and two lay brothers wait at the mine mouth; Odo sits up in the hand-cart, wrapped and steaming, and grips your hand as you pass. "The lights gathered near the fall when you carried me," he says quietly. "Like they wanted you to leave. Get him quick."

Then it's dark again, the two of you, the rails humming under dwarven boots. You lead, Veylin a pace behind, and your lantern lights his eyes steady down at the ties. It takes half an hour to make the drift, and nothing shows itself the whole way. That may be the worst of it. When you reach the collapse, the gap is as it was, the pale light gone from beside it.

And the knocking has stopped.

Not "stopped like a man freed." There was no sound of digging, no voices. Just silence where three-and-a-breath-and-three has been the world's heartbeat since you first came down. The fall is a black cairn from floor to roof, torn through by that one man-sized gap, edges sharp as bone.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka lays a hand flat on the fallen stone and says quietly, "Toma, if you can hear me, knock once." He waits, then asks Veylin to hold the lantern low and keep his eyes down while he peers through the gap, keeping his own gaze on the floor and checking for a way through or a space beneath the fall.

You lay your palm on the cold stone, and the fall lies still under your hand like a cairn over a king.

"Toma. If you can hear me, knock once."

The mountain holds its breath. Then, from under the fall — deep, muffled, thick with rock between you — one knock.

Alive. The word goes through you like warm ale. Veylin breathes out slow beside you and murmurs a forge-proverb about iron not despairing in the quench.

But one knock does not tell you where, and the fall does not give up its shape easily. With your eyes kept low and the lantern hooded narrow, you lie flat and peer into the gap, stone cold against your jaw, breath fogging back into your face. The truth is you can't make it out well — the lighting is against you, the angles worse, and after three lights' worth of eyes-down discipline your depth-sight through that black gap is worth little. The gap is man-sized, yes — you already knew that, edges said it. Whether it's big enough for mail and a guard's shoulders, whether the fall is wedged and settled over it or merely leaning its weight till something joggles it, you honestly cannot say. The one thing you get clearly, and it's the thing that mattered: a faint draught of air on your cheek, moving through the gap out toward you. Beyond the fall is open space, and it breathes.

Veylin, hands still down, says quietly: "I can pray over the stones for the Father's sight — a small blessing, a minute's work — it'd give us the lay of what's ahead. Or I could pray it over you, if you mean to go through; the old rite against fiends and spirits has kept temple men out of harm I'd rather not name. Or we keep it simple: your mail comes off your back, the rope goes round your waist, and you squeeze through like a stoveworm while I stand here and mind the dark." A pause. "I have three such blessings left in me tonight, and I don't mind which way you spend them. I only mind spending all three at once."

From under the fall, faint: one more knock. Impatient, almost.

What does Brakka do?

Brakka calls through the gap, "Hold on, Toma, we're coming, keep knocking if you can." Then to Veylin: "Bless the stones first for the lay of it, friend, and keep the other two in reserve. I'll tie the rope round my waist and take the mail off only if the gap won't pass me in it, with you holding the line and your eyes on the floor."

"Temple?" he croaks, staring at your hand as told, tears cutting clean tracks down a dust-grey face. "Real temple. Not the pretty ones. Say it again."

With the wall leaning over you and your boots set in scree, you heave the way you'd swing a sledge at a stuck bloom — a smith's whole body in it, timed, patient. The slab climbs. Toma hauls with his freed arm, and by the Father's knuckles, he slides free of the worst of it — chest and belly clear, dragged up beside you on the rubble. His legs are still wedged from the knees, but he's half out and breathing whole breaths, and through the gap behind you Veylin's voice comes steady, low, eyes down as bidden: "Heard the stone sing, brother. Is that good news or bad?" — waiting on your word to haul.

Then, in the pause while you chose the words to answer him, Toma's grip on your arm tightens to hurting. He isn't looking at your hand anymore. His eyes have gone past your shoulder, down the drift, wide.

"Behind you," he says, hardly a sound. "It heard the stone."

The shadow is no longer against the far wall. It stands out in the open now, in the seam's glow, tall and thin and patient as stone — and it is facing you. The pale light of it, separate somehow from the seam's glow, begins to strengthen, quietly, the way a lamp turns up: not bright enough to dazzle. Just bright enough to be worth looking at. And beyond it, farther down the drift where the glow thickens toward the deep stair, a second light kindles in the dark, and a third, spaced along the wall like the teeth of a trap.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

"Home," Toma repeats, like a man tasting the word. "Aye. Home."

Getting him through the gap takes joint effort of a kind no hymn celebrates — cloak-wrapped, rope under his arms, Veylin hauling with his back and Brakka's shield-hand steadying the shins while you both pretend nobody is swearing at a hundred-year-old slab — but the Father was generous with Veylin's shoulders, and the lantern keeps steady discipline the whole while, and at last Toma is out on the near side, and the seam's glow is a smear of pale in the dark behind you, silent, unwatching.

At the mine mouth, night has thickened and frozen. Odo sits up in his cart at the sound of you, and when Toma's shivering shape comes into the lantern-light the two miners make a sound you'll not repeat to Hessa, and grip each other like matchwood. The lay brothers have broth, and a brazier-pot of coals, and a sledge for stretchers, and between the four strong hands of the temple you need do nothing but stand guard and let them work.

Veylin answers you while the brothers lash Toma to the sledge. "Two," he says, holding up his fingers. "Two prayers. The Father's healing for a man who's bleeding his last, or the ward-rite for a man walking where the faithless walk — that one I'd keptwise reserve for the deep stair, if we go down it, because 'the faithless dark' has been walking about tonight wearing a man's own shape." He rubs his frost-scarred knuckles. "That's the count, brother smith. And by the count, and by the sunrise, I'll go where you go. I'd only say this: take ten breaths first and let the mountain see us standing still. A forge Shoped in a hurry makes cracked iron."

The temple hands will take Toma and Odo up to Hessa, with word of everything — Merrick included. After that, you and Veylin, two prayers in one pocket and a lantern burning three hours yet, and some ten hours of night: the workings are yours until sunrise and the council's bricks.

Toma catches your wrist as they lift the sledge. He speaks very low and sane and tired. "The stair's a hundred steps to the old pump-room. That's where we were sent. (You still carry the first sample-box — the one off the seventeenth step — and the crowbar; the Corbray hand-lamp stayed at the temple with Hessa, cleaned and waiting.)

You say his name, and the humming stops.

For three heartbeats the pump chamber is dead quiet, water ticking somewhere in the old wheel-race. Then Merrick turns his head — only his head, body still kneeling, spine bowed under the seam's glow — and it turns too far, the way an owl's does, past the point where necks stop. His face is grey-white and hollow, three days of beard frosted like the others' was, and his eyes when they find the sound of you don't find you: they look through, at the shape of a doorway that isn't there, at something behind the world. "Temple," he says. Not to you — testing the word, like a man biting a coin. "Toma. Odo." A pause, and then, in a tone of happy, terrible confidence, like a child correcting a grown-up: "No. You're not real. The pretty ones said. They said: the ones who come up the stair aren't real anymore." He smiles with dry lips. "But they said you'd say this. They told me, if a temple-shape comes, you keep filling boxes. Don't stop filling boxes. He pays. He pays for each one that's full." His hand goes on turning the shining sliver slowly, patiently. Root, thread, root.

He has stopped hearing his own name. He is hearing yours.

You edge along the chamber wall toward his back, hooded lantern spilled flat on the floor, eyes on his boots and the pale root-lines running out from his knees in the wet. Ten paces of quiet; Veylin matches you on the stair side, warhammer loose in hand, breathing slow. You also see the floor. The pale root-lines from his knees run five feet now, and the nearest shoots are not lying in the wet. They're lifting. Just off the stone, tips questing, breathing pale, and all their slow blind turning is toward the same direction — not toward the seam, and not toward the lights. Toward the neighborhood of your own boots.

Brakka stops dead and steps back out of reach of the lifting root-lines, keeping his eyes on the floor. "Veylin, the roots are turning toward me. Keep your boots out of the wet, and be ready to spend that ward-rite if they follow."

He tosses the cloak over Merrick's head from range and, if the man lets it fall, hooks the cloak's edge with the crowbar to drag him back from the wet toward dry stone and the stair.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

It is a strange, ugly little fight, the kind bards will never once sing of: a dwarf and a priest against weeds.

Your longsword swings into the pale tangle before you and finds it weirdly glancing — the shoots lean with the blade like grass in wind, your edge parting them in a spray of cold sap that whitens the stone before you, and you rear back at your miss — and the thing, whatever it feels, feels enough to fight for its footing.

The clumps rake at you and Veylin like a hundred cats' claws dragged cold across mail and shield — and find nothing to bite. Even Roots, you'd swear, do worse against dwarven iron than dwarven patience. Veylin, God bless the man's calm, steps backward up onto the dry steps as ordered, shield covering Merrick's hooded shape and boots clear of the wet, and smashes his Warhammer down on the nearest clump — whole branches burst grey-pale and spatter, and it shrinks on itself, sagging, half-broken.

The chamber's lights have gathered closer together over the drain, all a dozen in a knot now, a congregation of lamps with no holders, their shine thinning and intensifying and flaring in a slow rhythm. They do not approach you. Not yet. Beneath the shaking floor, further, the sound of stone shifting has grown closer to a sound of stone awaking.

The way up the stair is clear behind you, Merrick's knot of collapsed body included. The wet floor and Merrick's neat row of full brass boxes are behind the weeds before you.

Hill dwarf fighter, former temple guard of Greyhollow for six years. Acolyte of the Anvil Father.

Sealed mine workings beneath Greyhollow's mountain, closed off a generation ago. Three miners went down three days ago and never returned; a fourth came up babbling of lights that walk, and died before dawn.
Three miners of Greyhollow who went down into the old north workings three days ago and did not come back.
A miner who came up alone out of the old north workings last night, babbling about lights that walk, and died before dawn.
Hessa has asked Brakka to go down into the old north workings before the council bricks the entrance at sunrise and bring back whoever can still be brought back.
The god honored in Greyhollow: patron of smiths and the forge, worshipped at the Temple of the Anvil Father. The dead of the town are buried with hammer-signs on their eyes.

The dying fourth miner's words: "lights that walk." Brakka has now seen one — a small pale light, starlight-through-ice colored, hanging lamp-height in the old north workings. It sways like a lamp but doesn't flicker like flame, and it keeps its distance.

One of the three missing miners. His footprints shortened as he watched something; his body was dragged sidelong to the gallery's far end. Found there alive but entranced, cold, whispering that the "light is pretty."

A glittering vein in the rock of the old north workings, glowing faintly with a pale inner light. The soot warning on the gallery wall read: "THE SEAM IS A LIE." It somehow draws the lights that walk — or is drawn on by them.
A Greyhollow miner, trapped under a collapse in the old north workings, knocking three-and-pause for two days.
A Greyhollow miner who followed the glowing seam downhill into the deeper old workings, past where the lights came out of the wall.
A dwarf of Greyhollow and a temple hand of the Anvil Father; a strong, steady man of middle years who has hauled enough rock to know how to pick a wall apart.

The old mine-master of Greyhollow's sealed north workings, long dead; his ledger-chest is kept in the temple vestry. Hessa believes it may tell what was found a generation ago that got the workings closed.

The one who paid Merrick to bring back "what shone" from the old workings: a hidden employer, grey-gloved, no face seen, coin not miner's coin. Toma glimpsed a small mark on the glove's clasp: a circle with a balance-scales inside it.
A miner of the old north workings' first crews, sixty years back. His hand-lamp — scratched with his name — was found standing in the workings by Brakka, generations after the crews went below.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

attacks: Longsword: +4 to hit, 1d8+4 slashing (Dueling +2 included: one-handed, no other weapon); 1d10+2 two-handed (versatile)
Crossbow, light: +2 to hit, 1d8 piercing; range 80/320 (ammunition, loading, two-handed)
Unarmed strike: +4 to hit, 3 bludgeoning
features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Fighting Style: You adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. Choose one of the following options. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. CHOSEN: Fighting Style: Dueling.

Second Wind: You have a limited well of stamina that you can draw on to protect yourself from harm. On your turn, you can use a bonus action to regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your fighter level. Once you use this feature, you must finish a short or long rest before you can use it again.
Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Fighting Style: You adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. Choose one of the following options. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. CHOSEN: Fighting Style: Dueling.

Second Wind: You have a limited well of stamina that you can draw on to protect yourself from harm. On your turn, you can use a bonus action to regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your fighter level. Once you use this feature, you must finish a short or long rest before you can use it again.
Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

Greyhollow hangs on the mountainside like a lantern on a nail — a mining town of slate roofs and smoke, where the Anvil Father is honored in every forge-song and the dead are buried with hammer-signs on their eyes. For six years Brakka Ironvein stood guard at its temple, and if the work was quiet, it was honest. Quiet is over now.

Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, sealed since Brakka's grandsire's time. None came back. Last night a fourth man climbed out of that dark alone, raving about "lights that walk," and died before dawn with the words still on his lips. The town council has no patience left for ghosts: at sunrise tomorrow, they brick the entrance shut, living miners or not.

So the prior, old Hessa, came to Brakka with a lantern and a plain request. Bring back whoever can still be brought back. Before the mortar dries.

Now it is late afternoon, the light going copper and low. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a black square cut into grey rock, the borrowed hooded lantern in one hand and its flame guttering in the cold wind that comes up out of the hill — a wind that smells faintly of wet iron. Around the entrance, the council's masons have already stacked brick and mortar for the morning. Inside: timber shoring, old rail lines half-buried in rubble, and darkness your eyes can't shape.

What does Brakka do?

content.text: 10 minutes later: Day 1, 5:20 PM; timer Hooded lantern (borrowed, lit): 6 hours

The wind swallows your prayer, but the Anvil Father has heard worse from you, and you know the old dwarf's habit of noticing.

The lantern's oil is better than half full — Hessa filled it herself — and the hood throws a clean circle of light when you open it. The mine mouth was sealed with a dry-stone wall, and it's been pulled down from the inside edge, loose stones scattered outward onto the track. You crouch over the rails.

You're no tracker, but a mine floor is honest ground. You make out boot prints in the dust between the sleepers: two sets walking in, side by side, then a third a step behind, heavier. Five, six strides, and the dark takes them. What you don't see is harder to miss — no prints coming back. Just one set, deep and staggering, heels dug in, going out. Someone walked out of here last night by main strength. Beyond the drip line your light falls on a scatter of broken shale and old timber shoring, and beyond that the tunnel bends left and down.

You step in. Ten paces and the daylight behind you is a coin of copper; twenty and it's a Memory. The wind dies at the bend, and in the quiet there's water somewhere below, a slow tapping, and — when you stop to let your ears work — something else. Far down and faint, a rhythmic scrape, like a shovel or a boot-drag on stone. It stops. It does not start again while you listen.

The tunnel slopes gently down, rails half-swallowed by rubble, the roof good dwarven work — old but sound. Twenty yards in, wedged in a crack in the wall, you find the first sign of the miners: a hand-lamp, its oil burned out, abandoned upright like a man meant to come back for it.

The gallery answers you with a word.

You step through the gate, and your call goes down twenty yards of honest dwarework and comes back with nothing living in it. No answering knock from in here. But your ears, sharpened by twenty minutes of that mountain's silence, catch where the knocking actually lives: not down this gallery's length but through the rock, as if the knocker were somewhere beyond the collapse the pale light guards, under the broken stone that lies between you and it. The same rhythm. Three, a held breath, three. Patient. Continued.

The prints tell their story plainly now. Three men walked in, spread out, working — boot heels worn in a steady tramp along the left rail. Then, a quarter of the way in, something changes. A scuff-turn, feet planted wide. Two sets of prints stand close together for a stride. And the third man's prints never go past that — his last few strides shorten, like a man slowing down while he watched something. From there, there are no more prints of his at all. Just a brushed line through the dust, wide as two boots dragged sidelong, faintly toward the gallery's far dark.

The pick was laid down by a careful man. And by the wall where he stopped, at exactly the height of a dwarf's resting knuckles, the rock is smeared with soot — and the soot carries words, drawn in a thick, shaking hand:

DO NOT FOLLOW THE LIGHTS

The same hand, smaller, under it: THE SEAM IS A LIE

Out at the drift, the pale light still hangs by the gap in the collapse. It hasn't followed you in here. And the knocking goes on beneath your feet: three, a breath, three — the way a tired man signals that he is still alive.

The drag line runs the gallery's length, steady, unhurried, past empty ore-carts and a roofed stretch where the shoring is undercut with old tool marks. Your lantern pools on the floor ahead. And at the gallery's dead end you find him.

He sits against the rock with his back straight, hands in his lap, like a man resting after shift. A human, young, beard gone white with frost, hair frosted too, in a miner's leathers. He is alive — you see the slow fog of his breath — but there is frost on his lips that his breath does not melt. His eyes are open, fixed on the wall beside him, and they do not move when your light falls on them.

You follow his gaze to the wall, and your stomach drops to your boots. The rock is veined. A seam of grey-white stone runs branching through it like winter lightning, and the whole of it glows from within — the same color as the pale light. It doesn't shimmer like mineral caught in a flame. It glows, gently, as if lit from a room behind the stone. Beautiful, if you let it be. Your dwarf's bones know stone, and these workings should hold nothing like it.

The miner doesn't seem to hear his name when you mean to speak it. His lips move. You lean close. He is whispering, over and over, barely a sound: "It's pretty. Don't look away. It's pretty. Don't look away." He is cold as the wall. Frost has built on the folds of his clothes, thick, as if his breath had been freezing on him for hours. And away at the gallery's far end, from beneath your feet, the knocking under the rock still goes on: three, a breath, three.

He's alive, but he cannot walk, and the rock he worships is beside him.

Under the cloak the man steadies a little — the dark helps him, it seems, and having something warm over him helps more. "Odo," he says. "Odo Marsh. Trench-gang, second shift." His teeth chatter between the words. "Toma's under the fall at the drift's end — past the gap. The wall came down on him last night... I heard him knock through the stone all yesterday. Merrick went down the deep stair, where the seam runs thick. I told him — we all told him — the vein was wrong, it wasn't in any assay, and it glowed, and Father's blessings, it glowed like something breathing." He starts shuddering again. "The stair's past the fall's far side. There was a way around — an old air-shaft — but Merrick had to squeeze past the gap to reach it, and he looked up, right into one of the lights, and it... was with him after that. Walking behind him. I saw it. Then he stopped answering."

Odo tells you the rest fast, as if spending words now, while he can: the air-shaft route around the collapse is narrow — no room for a dwarf in mail, but rope could be thrown down to Toma's level — but working the wall of the fall itself would take a dozen men and half a day, and he thinks there may be a gap, a man-sized gap under it where the rock fell bridged. He isn't sure. He was running when he saw it.

"There are three lights, at least," he says, gripping your vambrace again. "They take a while to... gather. When I ran up the slope, they didn't chase. They aren't fast. They just wait, and they're patient, patient as stone."

When his words are spent, you haul him up. He weighs like a wet sack, and his shivering runs right through your shoulders. With his cloak over his head, his sight shaded from the drift's mouth, you step out.

At the gallery mouth, the pale light is there, and it's moved. It no longer hangs at the gap in the collapse. It has drifted back up-slope, past the old ore-cart, halfway between you and the way out — and there's another now, farther, a faint twin at the very edge of your lantern's reach. And a third. Near now, closer than either, only three yards off, hanging motionless above the rails, at eye height, waiting for a face to look at it.

You give the lights the courtesy they were fishing for: none at all. Eyes on the ties, shield edge up like a blinder, Odo's weight shifting with every step, you walk the rails up-slope.

It's the longest walk of your six years in this town. The near light drifts alongside you — you see it only as a pale stain at the rim of your vision, just past the shield's edge — and it stays with you a dozen yards, patient, swaying gently. Once it comes so close the light of it warms the back of your hand, and once you hear something — not a voice, a sound like slow breathing through a crack, getting a half-step ahead, as if it were looking for somewhere to be seen from. You keep your eyes on the iron. So do the rails. And the slope goes up.

It tries one trick: it swings out ahead of you and hangs low over the track, right where you must look to see your footing. But it doesn't bank on dwarves. Dwarves count ties, and pattern is pattern — you walk blind-true by the rail's hum under your boot and the memory of every sleeper you crossed coming down. The moment passes. The lights let you go.

Maybe they simply let you, and that is the worst thought of the walk. But nothing touches you, and nothing touches Odo, and his shivering under your hands is a live man's shivering.

Ten minutes past the bend, you feel the wind before you believe it, and then the mine mouth's black square has stars in it, and you are out. Night has come down while you were below, and the cold outside is a friend after the cold in the rock. Bricks wait in their stacks. The masons have gone home to supper, lantern-bearers' windows shine in Greyhollow above, and the temple is a ten-minute climb through town lanes, its forge-window lit — Hessa keeps late hours.

You set Odo down against a stack of council brick, wrapped in your cloak, and he clutches your arm with both hands now, strength coming back as fear goes. "Hessa," he says through chattering teeth. "Get her. Tell her — three lights, and they've got the deep workings, and Toma's under the fall, and the seam is the worst of it. Tell her Merrick took samples. He had them in his satchel, brass sample-boxes."

Sunrise is a little under eleven hours away.

"The Anvil Father keep you, Odo — I'll be back before the mortar's mixed." He nods up at you, wrapped like a bundle of washing against the brick stack, and you go up the lanes at a smith's jog, boots ringing on frozen cobbles, lamplit windows sliding past overhead.

The temple's side door latch lifts to your hand — six years of right. The forge-room is warm, the banked fire breathing, and it's Hessa you find first, as you knew you would: awake, at her desk over parish rolls, spectacles pushed up into white braids. She listens the way the old do, without interruption, while you give it all — the prints, the soot warning, the seam, Odo's trance, three lights, Toma's knocking, Merrick gone down the deep stair with brass sample-boxes.

The sample-boxes stop her like a nail driven flush. "Rocks that shine in the dark," she says slowly, taking her spectacles down. "There's a hymn the old folk stopped singing before your grandsire was whelped, about lights in the north galleries, and men following them and coming back wrong. I thought it was a way of teaching children to keep out of bad air." She looks at you for a long moment. "Fetch Master Stoner's ledger-chest from the vestry, then. No — first things first."

First things, by Hessa's ordering: two lay brothers go down the hill with cloaks, a hand-cart and a brazier-pot of broth for Odo at once. From the guard-store she gives you what you asked for: a second good rope, two picks, a sledge, wedges, and three crowbars. And she does not stop there — she lays a hand on the shoulder of a broad, quiet dwarf who had come in on the bell-hour to bank the forge: Veylin, a temple hand of your own watch, whom you've shared lamplight with on night rounds for years, and the strongest back in the parish. He hears the whole thing, rubs his beard once, and says only: "I was born to this kind of foolishness, then," and starts pulling his coat on.

"And the council," Hessa says, harder now. "Sunrise is sunrise and their word is their word, but you'll have me behind you tonight, and every hammer in the temple. Go. The clock's yours. Master Stoner's ledger and the old hymn will be waiting when you're back for them."

Downstairs, Hessa's letter sits before the council's head — the town will know by midnight that the temple claims the mine mouth, and lives may lie buried in it.

content.text: entry Master Stoner (person) created; relationship [49] added to Master Stoner; relationship [50] added to Master Stoner

Hessa thinks while you load the tools, then shakes her head. "Turning back. If the hymn said, Brakka, would a mine have been sealed with the words still in everyone's mouth?" She recites a fragment anyway, from somewhere deep: "'Keep to the wholesome dark, ye dwarrows all; the glitter that breathes is not thy father's spark; look to the anvil, not the bed of ore.'" She shrugs, small and old. "Advice, not remedy. But Master Stoner closed the north workings himself, and wrote why, somewhere in that chest. If a thing drives glitter back, he would have noted it, because he'd have had to live beside it. Get it when you come up — or send Veylin for it if you're loath to leave."

"And the lamp — done." A lay brother already has it out of your pack, wire brush in hand; by the time you've shouldered the ropes she calls him over and squints at the cleaned base. Her face goes strange. She says one word — "Corbray" — and sets the lamp down softly, as if it were heavy. "That's the name scratched there. Corbray. Older than Toma's whole family. That lamp went down with the first crews a generation back. Which means somebody was down there before the miners, Brakka — or something kept a lamp for sixty years."

She doesn't follow that thought any further, and neither should you, tonight. "Go. The Father walks with the thorough."

Veylin falls in beside you — chain mail, shield, warhammer, a sledge over one shoulder, calm as a feed trough — and repeats your rule back to you word for word, which is how you know it took: "Eyes to the floor. If I feel pretty, I look at you."

Broth and brazier and two lay brothers wait at the mine mouth; Odo sits up in the hand-cart, wrapped and steaming, and grips your hand as you pass. "The lights gathered near the fall when you carried me," he says quietly. "Like they wanted you to leave. Get him quick."

Then it's dark again, the two of you, the rails humming under dwarven boots. You lead, Veylin a pace behind, and your lantern lights his eyes steady down at the ties. It takes half an hour to make the drift, and nothing shows itself the whole way. That may be the worst of it. When you reach the collapse, the gap is as it was, the pale light gone from beside it.

And the knocking has stopped.

Not "stopped like a man freed." There was no sound of digging, no voices. Just silence where three-and-a-breath-and-three has been the world's heartbeat since you first came down. The fall is a black cairn from floor to roof, torn through by that one man-sized gap, edges sharp as bone.

What does Brakka do?

content.text:
You lay your palm on the cold stone, and the fall lies still under your hand like a cairn over a king.

"Toma. If you can hear me, knock once."

The mountain holds its breath. Then, from under the fall — deep, muffled, thick with rock between you — one knock.

Alive. The word goes through you like warm ale. Veylin breathes out slow beside you and murmurs a forge-proverb about iron not despairing in the quench.

But one knock does not tell you where, and the fall does not give up its shape easily. With your eyes kept low and the lantern hooded narrow, you lie flat and peer into the gap, stone cold against your jaw, breath fogging back into your face. The truth is you can't make it out well — the lighting is against you, the angles worse, and after three lights' worth of eyes-down discipline your depth-sight through that black gap is worth little. The gap is man-sized, yes — you already knew that, edges said it. Whether it's big enough for mail and a guard's shoulders, whether the fall is wedged and settled over it or merely leaning its weight till something joggles it, you honestly cannot say. The one thing you get clearly, and it's the thing that mattered: a faint draught of air on your cheek, moving through the gap out toward you. Beyond the fall is open space, and it breathes.

Veylin, hands still down, says quietly: "I can pray over the stones for the Father's sight — a small blessing, a minute's work — it'd give us the lay of what's ahead. Or I could pray it over you, if you mean to go through; the old rite against fiends and spirits has kept temple men out of harm I'd rather not name. Or we keep it simple: your mail comes off your back, the rope goes round your waist, and you squeeze through like a stoveworm while I stand here and mind the dark." A pause. "I have three such blessings left in me tonight, and I don't mind which way you spend them. I only mind spending all three at once."

From under the fall, faint: one more knock. Impatient, almost.

What does Brakka do?

10 minutes later: Day 1, 8:05 PM

You call to Toma, and the knock that answers is two now — still weak, but quicker, like a man who's stopped conserving himself.

Veylin is honest about his tools, being Veylin. "The sight-prayer you're thinking of isn't mine to give — that's for adepts with grey in their beards. What I have is a workman's blessing, a steady hand and a strong back for one breath of time. Hold still." He speaks the words over you quietly, the old forge-cadence, thumb marking your mailed shoulder with the hammer-sign. Then he kneels at the gap foot with the rope end and your lantern angled low, eyes on the ties, and pays out line as you go.

The gap takes you — barely, mail and all, with scraping and a moment where the shield has to go through flat ahead of you, shoved by its strap, and your ribs and a hundred-year-old slab introduce themselves. But dwarves are built for the country God made them for. You come through into a low void on the fall's far side: a drift that was a working gallery until last night, half-choked with the downcome, floor first raised and then dropped away. Beyond your lantern, drafts move. It isn't a dead pocket at all.

The knocking is loud in here — close, and no longer through stone. You track it down a slope of loose rubble to a wall of fallen slabs, and there he is: a hand and forearm out of the gap between slabs, knuckles worn raw from knocking, work-callused, moving. Scraps of a voice come through — a youngish voice, cracked with shouting days of it, saying the same words over and over: "…still here… I'm still here…"

He is pinned from the chest down, well-wedged. Alive; not a promise you'd make about his legs. There's space to work — a slab or two could be barred and lifted, with two strong backs and luck, but the rubble wall leans and you are one side of it with Veylin the rope's length away on the other, the gap between you no wider than it was.

Beyond the pinned man's feet, farther down the drift, the darkness is not quite dark. A pale sheen lies along the far wall, the way snow-glow lies on a night field. This close, the seam is beautiful, there's no lying about it, branching silver in the stone, breathing light. Right at the edge of that glow, a shadow stands against the wall — tall, wrong-jointed, the silhouette of a man rendered by someone who'd only had a man described — motionless, facing into the seam's light. It does not move while your lantern holds. Nowhere on it can you see a face, though it has the place for one.

What does Brakka do?

content.text:
You call to Toma, and the knock that answers is two now — still weak, but quicker, like a man who's stopped conserving himself.

"Then stones it is," Veylin says, and kneels with his hand flat on the fallen rock, speaking the forge-cadence words in a murmur — for the Father's sight, for the lay of what's ahead. To your own surprise, what the blessing mostly gives you is steady hands and a strong back for the squeeze: whatever the Father shows of stone, He shows it to a man who lives to use it. "One spent," Veylin says as it settles, "two left in me — keep that count when you choose." He kneels at the gap's foot with the rope end and your lantern angled low, eyes on the ties, and pays out line as you go.

The gap takes you — barely, mail and all, with scraping and a moment where the shield has to go through flat ahead of you, shoved by its strap, and your ribs and a hundred-year-old slab introduce themselves. But dwarves are built for the country the Father made them for. You come through into a low void on the fall's far side: a drift that was a working gallery until two days back, half-choked with the downcome, floor first raised and then dropped away. Beyond your lantern, drafts move. It isn't a dead pocket at all.

The knocking is loud in here — close, and no longer through stone. You track it down a slope of loose rubble to a wall of fallen slabs, and there he is: a hand and forearm out of the gap between slabs, knuckles worn raw from knocking, work-callused, moving. Scraps of a voice come through — a youngish voice, cracked with shouting days of it, saying the same words over and over: "…still here… I'm still here…"

He is pinned from the chest down, well-wedged. Alive; not a promise you'd make about his legs. There's space to work — a slab or two could be barred and lifted, with two strong backs and luck, but the rubble wall leans and you are one side of it with Veylin the rope's length away on the other, the gap between you no wider than it was.

Beyond the pinned man's feet, farther down the drift, the darkness is not quite dark. A pale sheen lies along the far wall, the way snow-glow lies on a night field. This close, the seam is beautiful, there's no lying about it, branching silver in the stone, breathing light. Right at the edge of that glow, a shadow stands against the wall — tall, wrong-jointed, the silhouette of a man rendered by someone who'd only had a man described — motionless, facing into the seam's light. It does not move while your lantern holds. Nowhere on it can you see a face, though it has the place for one.

What does Brakka do?

content.text:
Your crowbar bites, the slab grates, and Toma's raw-knuckled hand closes on your wrist like a drowning man's.

"Temple?" he croaks, staring at your hand as told, tears cutting clean tracks down a dust-grey face. "Real temple. Not the pretty ones. Say it again."

With the wall leaning over you and your boots set in scree, you heave the way you'd swing a sledge at a stuck bloom — a smith's whole body in it, timed, patient. The slab climbs. Toma hauls with his freed arm, and by the Father's knuckles, he slides free of the worst of it — chest and belly clear, dragged up beside you on the rubble. His legs are still wedged from the knees, but he's half out and breathing whole breaths, and through the gap behind you Veylin's voice comes steady, low, eyes down as bidden: "Heard the stone sing, brother. Is that good news or bad?" — waiting on your word to haul.

Then, in the pause while you chose the words to answer him, Toma's grip on your arm tightens to hurting. He isn't looking at your hand anymore. His eyes have gone past your shoulder, down the drift, wide.

"Behind you," he says, hardly a sound. "It heard the stone."

The shadow is no longer against the far wall. It stands out in the open now, in the seam's glow, tall and thin and patient as stone — and it is facing you. The pale light of it, separate somehow from the seam's glow, begins to strengthen, quietly, the way a lamp turns up: not bright enough to dazzle. Just bright enough to be worth looking at. And beyond it, farther down the drift where the glow thickens toward the deep stair, a second light kindles in the dark, and a third, spaced along the wall like the teeth of a trap.

There's room between the slabs and the downcomer wall: enough to fight a dwarf's fight, back to the rubble, if it comes to that. And the gap to Veylin's side — a squeeze, but a way out — a rope's length away, with Toma half-pinned between you and it.
