RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

content.text:
It happens fast, the way disasters and rescues do.

You drive the crowbar and the second slab climbs — your shoulders burning, Toma moaning and pulling with both arms — and his legs come free with a scrape of torn boot-leather. Not crushed, by the Father's mercy: bruised black and bloodied, but his. He sags against you, shaking, and you shout for Veylin to haul.

And the shadow steps closer.

You feel it before anything: warmth leaving your back like a door opened on winter. You spin, shield up — and the thing is on you, longer arms than any man, a blackness of a hand that drinks the lantern's circle as it comes. It rakes at you and you catch the blow on your shield, the wood going cold under your arm where it strikes, cold enough to burn.

Then the gap behind you fills with chrome-grey beard. Veylin — haul line forgotten, having wedged his own broad carcass through the fall on the sound of stone — plants his feet beside you, will not look anywhere but your boots going past, and puts out one hand in the hammer-sign. "The Father's fire, by His forge," he says, calm as ever, "the wholesome flame on the faithless dark." Light falls out of his palm like a struck spark from the anvil — clean, white, warm — and takes the shadow full in its faceless place.

(You still carry the first sample-box — the one off the seventeenth step — and the crowbar; the Corbray hand-lamp stayed at the temple with Hessa, cleaned and waiting.)

You say his name, and the humming stops.

For three heartbeats the pump chamber is dead quiet, water ticking somewhere in the old wheel-race. Then Merrick turns his head — only his head, body still kneeling, spine bowed under the seam's glow — and it turns too far, the way an owl's does, past the point where necks stop. His face is grey-white and hollow, three days of beard frosted like the others' was, and his eyes when they find the sound of you don't find you: they look through, at the shape of a doorway that isn't there, at something behind the world. His lips are cracked and his voice comes out in pieces.

"Temple," he says. Not to you — testing the word, like a man biting a coin. "Toma. Odo." A pause, and then, in a tone of happy, terrible confidence, like a child correcting a grown-up: "No. You're not real. The pretty ones said. They said: the ones who come up the stair aren't real anymore." He smiles with dry lips. "But they said you'd say this. They told me, if a temple-shape comes, you keep filling boxes. Don't stop filling boxes. He pays. He pays for each one that's full." His hand goes on turning the shining sliver slowly, patiently. Root, thread, root.

He has stopped hearing his own name. He is hearing yours.

You edge along the chamber wall toward his back, hooded lantern spilled flat on the floor, eyes on his boots and the pale root-lines running out from his knees in the wet. Ten paces of quiet; Veylin matches you on the stair side, warhammer loose in hand, breathing slow. And as you come around Merrick's flank — close now, six feet, cloak gathered in your left hand — you can see the row of brass boxes before him, every one open, and every one neatly filled with little branching fingers of the shining vein, broken off and sorted by size, a merchant's care in every box.

You also see the floor. The pale root-lines from his knees run five feet now, and the nearest shoots are not lying in the wet. They're lifting. Just off the stone, tips questing, breathing pale, and all their slow blind turning is toward the same direction — not toward the seam, and not toward the lights. Toward the neighborhood of your own boots.

What does Brakka do?

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

The cloak flies true — a guard's toss, six years of drill in it — and settles over Merrick's head and shoulders like dark spilled over a lamp. The effect is instant and eerie: the humming stops, the shining sliver drops from his fingers, and the man goes slack, muttering, pliant as wet rope. You hook the cloak's edge with the crowbar and haul him backward out of the wet in one smith's pull, clear onto dry stone near the foot of the stair.

The pale lines in the wet do not like it.

Every root-shoot in reach stands up at once — white, translucent, branching, edged in vein-silver, like the fingers of the seam reaching out of stone into air — and the seam's glow flares hard enough that the water runs white with light. Around the chamber the hanging lights swing toward you like lanterns carried by hurrying hands, and from the drifts behind the old wheel, distant, comes the sound of stone shifting. Something far below noticed.

Six of the pale shoots — three small, wriggling clumps of them close by, and more thickening in the wet — rake at your boots and Veylin's, thin scratches like cat-claws but a hundred at a time, cold as the shadow's touch was cold. They are small, and they are weak, but you are standing in the doorway of their whole world's larder.

It's a fight now, small and mean and about feet, in the shadow of the great wheel — and by the fall of your own quick blood it is your move first.

What does Brakka do?

content.text:
It is a strange, ugly little fight, the kind bards will never once sing of: a dwarf and a priest against weeds.

Your longsword swings into the pale tangle before you and finds it weirdly glancing — the shoots lean with the blade like grass in wind, your edge parting them in a spray of cold sap that whitens the stone before you, and you rear back at your miss — and the thing, whatever it feels, feels enough to fight for its footing.

The clumps rake at you and Veylin like a hundred cats' claws dragged cold across mail and shield — and find nothing to bite. Even Roots, you'd swear, do worse against dwarven iron than dwarven patience. Veylin, God bless the man's calm, steps backward up onto the dry steps as ordered, shield covering Merrick's hooded shape and boots clear of the wet, and smashes his Warhammer down on the nearest clump — whole branches burst grey-pale and spatter, and it shrinks on itself, sagging, half-broken.

The chamber's lights have gathered closer together over the drain, all a dozen in a knot now, a congregation of lamps with no holders, their shine thinning and intensifying and flaring in a slow rhythm. They do not approach you. Not yet. Beneath the shaking floor, further, the sound of stone shifting has grown closer to a sound of stone awaking.

The way up the stair is clear behind you, Merrick's knot of collapsed body included. The wet floor and Merrick's neat row of full brass boxes are behind the weeds before you.

What does Brakka do?
